title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
abstract: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.

title: Riemannian Optimization on Unknown Manifolds via Stochastic Proximal Refinement
abstract: We study Riemannian optimization on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples. The central challenge is to turn feasible samples into optimization steps, i.e., the samples are drawn from the unknown feasible manifold, but do not directly provide the tangent spaces, projections, or retractions required by classic Riemannian methods. Moreover, regions with low objective values may be sparsely represented in the data, so directly sampling from a distribution fitted to these observations can require many draws to find better feasible solutions. We introduce Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds (PRISM), which turns feasible-sample access into an iterative optimization procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. Theoretically, we show that PRISM recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, leading to provable objective descent, feasibility (manifold adherence), and convergence toward first-order stationarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through synthetic experiments illustrating its geometric properties and applications to data-driven building control and diverse real world optimization tasks, highlighting its potential as a general framework for data-driven optimization across scientific and engineering domains.

title: Local Budget Benefits, Population Commitment, and Solver Performance: A DGO Case Study with Controlled DE Transfer
abstract: An evaluated candidate can improve a local search step, alter the population used by later steps, and affect a solver's final result. We distinguish these three questions using Da Gou Gun Optimization (DGO), a population optimizer designed for this study. Its JQ100 configuration evaluates an interpolation candidate during a two-sided probe. We define local budget value, population commitment effects and complete-policy performance, and give an exact example in which a locally better commitment leads to a worse continuation. Short-horizon matched comparisons favor interpolation on eligible quadratic states. Paired continuations yield mixed effect estimates, with primary group intervals spanning zero. Complete-policy comparisons favor JQ100 over the tested classical references in aggregate; a matched-start comparison has favorable means but intervals spanning parity. On 24 boxed BBOB functions, target-truncated geometric-mean error ratios favor JQ100 over the tested classical policies and favor L-SHADE and CMA-ES over JQ100 under the stated initialization and stopping rules. Local evaluation gains, commitment effects and solver competitiveness therefore require separate comparisons.

title: AERS-Pro: code, PII-masked corpus and per-sample predictions for Vietnamese e-commerce sentiment analysis
abstract: Research artifact accompanying the manuscript A Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Vietnamese Sentiment Analysis in E-Commerce (manuscript QNUJS-B2662, under review at the Journal of Science - Quy Nhon University). AERS-Pro is a stacking ensemble for three-class (negative / neutral / positive) Vietnamese review sentiment. It combines word TF-IDF, hashed character n-grams, lexicon and part-of-speech features, out-of-fold stacking of logistic regression, LinearSVC and LightGBM base learners, and conditional probability calibration. It is compared with a fine-tuned PhoBERT baseline over 10 seeds using group-aware (near-duplicate-safe) 60/20/20 splits. Contents: source code; a PII-masked corpus of 25,289 Vietnamese e-commerce reviews (phone numbers, URLs and social-media handles replaced by placeholders; personal names and addresses were not screened); per-sample predictions of both systems for all 10 seeds (row index, label, logits or probabilities; no review text); split audits; statistical tables (Nadeau-Bengio corrected tests, TOST, Holm adjustment); training logs; SHA-256 manifest. Review texts were collected from a public e-commerce platform for non-commercial research; the corpus is provided for research use only.

title: Fine-Tuning AraBert with BiLSTM and Layer-Freezing Strategies for Arabic AI-Generated Text Detection
abstract: أدى النمو السريع لنماذج اللغة الكبيرة (LLMs) إلى تحسين جودة النصوص العربية المُولّدة آليًا، مما خلق تحديات في التمييز بين المحتوى المُولّد بواسطة الذكاء الاصطناعي والنصوص المكتوبة يدويًا. تقدم هذه الورقة البحثية بنية للتعلم بالنقل للكشف عن النصوص العربية المُولّدة بواسطة الذكاء الاصطناعي، بالاعتماد على نموذج AraBERT المُدرّب مسبقًا مع رأس تصنيف BiLSTM. يدرس النهج المقترح كيفية تأثير ضبط المعلمات الفائقة وطرق تجميد طبقات المحوّل على أداء التصنيف. تم إعداد أربعة مجموعات للضبط الدقيق (G1, G2, G3, G4) من خلال تعديل الحد الأقصى لطول التسلسل، ومعدل التعلم، ودورات التدريب، والبعد الخفي لطبقة BiLSTM. وجرى اختبار كل مجموعة باستخدام ستة إعدادات لتجميد الطبقات، تراوحت بين الضبط الدقيق الكامل وتجميد الطبقات الإحدى عشرة الأولى من مُشفِّر AraBERT، مما نتج عنه 24 تركيبة تجريبية. وتم تقييم مقاييس الدقة والإحكام والاستدعاء ودرجة F1 على مجموعة التحقق ومجموعة اختبار خارجية مستقلة. أظهرت النتائج أن مجموعة G4-Freeze3 حققت أفضل أداء على مجموعة التحقق، بدقة 98.60% ودرجة F1 بلغت 98.64%، في حين حققت مجموعة G2-Freeze5 أفضل أداء على مجموعة الاختبار الخارجية، بدقة 99.22%، وإحكام 98.84%، واستدعاء 99.61%، ودرجة F1 بلغت 99.22%. علاوة على ذلك، أدت مجموعة G2-Freeze5 إلى خفض عدد المعلمات القابلة للتدريب من 136.11 مليون إلى 100.67 مليون مقارنةً بالضبط الدقيق الكامل، مع تحسين أداء التصنيف الخارجي. ومع ذلك، لوحظ أن التجميد الأعمق للطبقات غالبًا ما يؤدي إلى تراجع الأداء. وتُظهر هذه النتائج أن الجمع بين معلمات الضبط الدقيق وعمق التجميد يمكن أن يحقق توازنًا فعالًا بين أداء التصنيف وعدد المعلمات المدربة في الكشف عن النصوص العربية المُولَّدة آليًا.

title: When appearance and motion disagree: evaluating class-motion consistency against disguised uncrewed surface vessels
abstract: Defense systems for maritime assets must distinguish approaching benign craft from uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) with sufficient warning to act. Shore cameras using computer vision can separate hostile vessels from benign traffic, but these systems may be attacked using an adversarial hull patch or physical disguise. We evaluate adversarial hull patches and find they suppress detection in up to 29% of attempts but never cause misclassification as benign. Physical disguise, however, can bypass both a camera check and a radar presence check. To evaluate defenses, we develop a hybrid replay protocol from automatic identification system (AIS) tracks that combines recorded benign motion with direct or off-axis attack run-ins. We find that for recreational-labeled vessels attacking via direct run-in within 4 nautical miles, an asset-relative closing-rate check flags 94-95% at 15-20 knots, compared with 12% for a track-only speed check. The checks are complementary on off-axis approaches, constraining the attacker to remain below both thresholds and extending the time required to reach the asset. Flagging on either check has a 4.9% held-out false-alarm rate overall and 12.3% on recreational traffic. The replay-based evaluation protocol supports comparative test and evaluation of defense methods.

title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.

title: Ask on Demand: Targeted Peer Communication for Parallel Agentic Systems
abstract: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents' needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. We propose Ask on Demand (AOD), a communication framework that enables agents to seek targeted peer assistance when specific information needs arise. Upon an approved request, AOD retrieves relevant evidence from peer execution histories, selects a suitable peer, and generates a response tailored to the request. To determine when such assistance is worthwhile, we train a lightweight gate using paired team continuations, with supervision derived from final team outcomes and inference cost. Experiments on AppWorld and WebShop demonstrate that AOD consistently improves task performance over independent parallel execution while achieving lower inference cost than existing information-sharing baselines. These findings highlight the benefits of aligning peer communication with agents' evolving information needs to achieve more effective and efficient collaboration.

title: Replication package for: Verification-Gated Hybrid Negotiation for Decentralized Multi-Agent Planning under Temporal Uncertainty
abstract: This package contains the code, data and results needed to reproduce the experiments of the paper “Verification-Gated Hybrid Negotiation for Decentralized Multi-Agent Planning under Temporal Uncertainty.” The paper proposes Hybrid Flexibility Negotiation (HFN), a coordination framework in which agents with private temporal plans (Simple Temporal Networks with Uncertainty) repair a loss of dynamic controllability by escalating from direct negotiation to broker-mediated recommendations and then to a decentralized cascade. Every state is committed only after an exact dynamic-controllability check succeeds at every agent. The package includes: a Python implementation of the dynamic-controllability checker, the network and crisis generator, all negotiation strategies, and two distributed constraint-optimisation baselines; one script per experiment, a script that regenerates all tables and figures, and unit tests; the ICU length-of-stay table from the MIMIC-IV Clinical Database Demo used to calibrate durations (ODbL licence); all result files reported in the paper. All instances are generated from fixed random seeds. See README.md for instructions and for the mapping between scripts and research questions.

title: GLTF-FEDformer: an adaptive time-frequency fusion method for multivariate time series anomaly detection enhanced by prediction error embedding
abstract: Abstract Multivariate time series are widespread in scenarios such as industrial IoT, smart manufacturing, energy systems, and medical monitoring. Their anomalous behaviors often involve complex patterns like long-range dependency changes, local dynamic shifts, transient spectral perturbations, and variable-association mismatches. Existing reconstruction-based and attention-based methods can learn the overall evolution of normal sequences but still lack fine-grained characterization of local time-frequency changes; moreover, relying solely on point-wise prediction errors for anomaly scoring struggles to fully reflect structural shifts in the error distribution. To address these issues, this paper proposes GLTF-FEDformer, a multivariate time series anomaly detection method that jointly models global and local time-frequency features. The method learns temporal dependencies, trend changes, and periodic candidate patterns from long-window contexts via a global temporal representation module, and enhances the modeling of temporal evolution through a continuous dynamic refinement mechanism. It also builds a lightweight local time-frequency feature extraction module that uses short-time Fourier transform, 2D convolutions, spectral gating, and inverse transforms to enhance the perception of local morphological changes, spectral perturbations, and time-frequency coupled features within local windows. A gated fusion mechanism performs data-dependent integration of global temporal information and local time-frequency information to obtain more discriminative prediction representations. Additionally, we design an anomaly scoring strategy based on a prediction-error-embedded profile, mapping prediction residuals into an embedding space and measuring structural deviations of test prediction-error embeddings from the normal error profile through variable-level standardized distances. The profile score is further combined with point-wise prediction errors to form anomaly responses with temporal localization ability. This strategy not only uses amplitude information of prediction errors but also captures structural shifts of the error distribution relative to normal patterns, thereby improving detection robustness in complex anomaly scenarios. Experimental results show the proposed method effectively enhances multivariate time series anomaly recognition and demonstrates strong detection performance and stability across various public datasets.

title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

title: TSBPO: Tree-Structured Branching for Policy Optimization in Interactive Language Agents
abstract: Terminal feedback in multi-turn agent training leaves both rollout allocation and local credit underdetermined. Dynamics-Predictive Sampling (DPS) [9] provides a task-level predictive sampling reference, but interactive agents also need to choose which visited states merit further continuations. We introduce TSBPO with two method components. A lightweight, fine-grained Root/Branch budget allocator distributes factual rollouts across tasks and additional suffixes across replayable states using likelihood-fitted estimates of terminal-outcome contrast. On the resulting physical rollout trees, a tree-aware step-level credit assignment algorithm compares immediate sibling segments and assigns their local outcome contrasts to the turns they contain. Exact task/observation groups provide a complementary step term. The allocator selects what to sample; observed outcomes determine the subsequent credit. With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, fixed checkpoints attain 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld, and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for each of the 500 WebShop test goals. At the WebShop update-100 checkpoint, removing the observation-group step term yields 75.93% under the same evaluation. These results describe the evaluated training configurations on two interactive benchmarks.

title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings
abstract: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. To address this, model embeddings compress each model into a fixed-length vector from which many properties can be predicted. Existing methods, such as EmbedLLM, build these vectors from correctness patterns and question features, and often need large probe batteries to do so. However, many behaviors that are important when choosing a model, such as its verbosity, safety and style, show up more in how it answers than in whether it is correct. We introduce BULLPEN (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings), a framework that extends EmbedLLM in three ways. First, BULLPEN organizes the downstream tasks that prior work uses and adds 20 task benchmarks we built on behavior, style and provenance. Second, it is the first framework to read a model's own answer text jointly with its correctness and the question text. Third, it encodes models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool. Across 260 open-weight models, our answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder. Our encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from only 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute of the full question pool), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83% with the same 400 questions. Because these embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioral auditing and low-cost profiling, and could extend to API-only models. Code and data: https://github.com/wcquesera/bullpen

title: CIRCE Divines LLM Task Complexity from Constraint Structure
abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.

title: Artificial intelligence, emotional well-being, and difficult dialogues in school settings
abstract: Attention to students' emotional dimension represents a key determinant of both academic success and future personal and social development (Weber et al., 2016). Within this perspective, the design of emotionally meaningful learning experiences, including those supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based conversational technologies, can enhance students' well-being and engagement by recognizing emotions as a fundamental component of learning processes. Through Natural Language Processing techniques and affective computing models, intelligent conversational systems can detect and interpret users' emotional states and dynamically adapt interactions accordingly. title: Interpretable Deep Learning for Ovarian Cancer Subtype Classification Using Histopathology Images
abstract: Abstract Ovarian cancer is a histologically heterogeneous malignancy in which accurate subtype classification is essential for prognosis and treatment selection. Manual interpretation of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)–stained histopathology slides remains time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability, particularly for morphologically overlapping subtypes. In this study, an interpretable deep learning framework was developed for automated ovarian cancer subtype classification using a fine-tuned ResNet50 architecture. A publicly available histopathology dataset comprising five major ovarian carcinoma subtypes was employed. Model training incorporated optimized strategies including data augmentation, selective layer unfreezing, label smoothing, and test-time augmentation. Classification performance was benchmarked against established convolutional neural network architectures. Visual interpretability was assessed using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to examine model attention patterns. The proposed framework achieved high classification performance, with strong accuracy and macro-averaged F1-scores across subtypes. Grad-CAM analysis demonstrated that model attention was consistently localized to histologically relevant tissue regions in correctly classified samples, while misclassifications were associated with morphologically ambiguous structures. These findings suggest that classification errors primarily reflect intrinsic histopathologic overlap rather than spurious model behavior. Overall, this work establishes a reproducible and interpretable deep learning benchmark for ovarian cancer subtype classification and provides clinically meaningful insight into model decision processes. The proposed framework is well-suited for use as a second-reader decision support tool in digital pathology workflows.

title: From fleet trajectories to single-cell promises: hierarchically weighted conformal prediction for battery SOH monitoring
abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.

title: Queryable Gaussian View Index: Retrieval, Localization, and Agentic View Search
abstract: Given an existing 3D Gaussian scene and calibrated references, we seek camera poses and views that answer text, RGB, or image-and-instruction queries. RGB localization recovers a source camera; a target-view instruction can require a different camera while preserving the referenced scene content. Queryable Gaussian View Index (QGVI) supports these requests through a semantic view index that binds structured captions and observations to calibrated camera poses. QGVI-T retrieves indexed candidates with BM25. QGVI-A uses this interface and geometric source localization (QGVI-I) as tools, sharing candidate poses, observations, and query conditions marked satisfied, violated, or unknown. Unmet conditions guide camera proposals and rendered checks. Supported answers exit early; unresolved queries return insufficient evidence within a shared search budget. We construct a nine-scene benchmark, including city-scale environments, covering semantic view retrieval, RGB localization with out-of-map rejection, and image-conditioned target-view search. Under GPT assessment on the development cohort, QGVI-A returns confirmed correct views for 90.4\% of target-view queries, compared with 26.8\% for one-shot Retrieve + Select. This comparison evaluates complete policies with different information and call budgets; QGVI-A achieves higher coverage at lower answer precision. The benchmark separates semantic satisfaction, source-camera accuracy, and acceptance decisions.

title: Source code for: Virtual Immunohistochemical Staining for Pathological Complete Response Prediction in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract: This record contains the source code supporting both the article (submitted to Bioinformatics, 2026) and the master's dissertation (PPGCC/UFMG, 2026) entitled "Virtual Immunohistochemical Staining for Pathological Complete Response Prediction in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer". The project predicts pathological complete response (pCR) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) by combining H&E images with Ki-67 and PHH3 stains (real or virtually generated) through a biomarker-based spatial attention mechanism. Contents: bcs-kedro/ - Kedro project implementing the full pCR prediction pipeline: image preprocessing, generation of biomarker-based spatial attention maps, and a ResNet-based classifier with attention. virtual_staining/ - models for generating Ki-67 and PHH3 stains from H&E images, including CycleGAN, conditional GAN (cGAN), and diffusion-based approaches. Requirements: Python 3.8+, dependencies listed in requirements.txt. Training is GPU-optimized.ob scripts are configured for SLURM clusters. Installation and execution instructions are provided in README.md. Trained models: Hugging Face | Digital Pathology Models Source repository: Github | PCR Classification Repository Main author: Henrique Colonese Main contributor: Daniel Ayala

title: ipi-bench: a reproducible, utility aware benchmark for adaptive indirect prompt injection in multi document LLM screening
abstract: Code, configuration, synthetic corpus generator, attack taxonomy, defense implementations, metrics, statistics and figure scripts accompanying the manuscript 'Beyond Detection: A Reproducible, Utility Aware Benchmark for Adaptive Indirect Prompt Injection in Multi Document LLM Screening'. The archive includes an OpenAI compatible client for live runs, a documented synthetic responder for offline validation of the pipeline, the trial level results and aggregated tables of the reported run, the LaTeX source of the paper, and a Colab notebook. Results produced with the synthetic responder validate the pipeline and are not measurements of any real language model.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Initialization with Dual-Guided Inversion for Flow-Based Inverse Problem Solvers
abstract: Flow models have recently emerged as powerful generative priors for solving inverse problems. Despite their success, most existing flow-based inverse problem solvers initialize the reconstruction process with random Gaussian noise. However, recent studies in image generation have shown that the choice of initial noise can significantly influence generation outcomes. The role of initialization as a distinct design choice in flow-based inverse problem solving remains comparatively underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate noise initialization strategies while holding the downstream flow-based inverse solver fixed. We propose Retrieval-Augmented Initialization with Dual-Guided Inversion (RA-DGI), a method that constructs improved initial noise by leveraging retrieved proxy clean images and dual-guided inversion. Extensive experiments across multiple inverse problems demonstrate that the quality of the initial noise substantially affects reconstruction fidelity and perceptual performance. RA-DGI outperforms standard random initialization and achieves superior results compared to inference-time scaling strategies, while requiring less computational overhead. These findings highlight initialization as a critical yet previously overlooked factor in flow-based inverse problem solvers.

title: BURIDAN: the ambiguous picture, decided by a 144-qubit collective with its controller in the loop. A registered experiment
abstract: On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, 144 qubits form 36 domains of four. A field law running on a microcontroller (an ESP32-S3, firmware v4.12) turns the measured populations of every cycle into the rotation angles of the next, and a Hebbian coupling matrix of two images, a unicorn and a heart, makes the two images attractors of the collective: cued with part of either, the field completes it. The experiment writes a blend of the two: of the 16 pixels on which the images differ, k are taken from the unicorn and the rest from the heart (which pixels: fixed in the registration, per trial), the 20 shared pixels as they are. The blend is held for two cycles and released, and the field runs six free cycles on its own. Resolution is the first free cycle in which the field's majority picture agrees with one image on at least 90 percent of the pixels. Lines, thresholds and rules were fixed and hashed before the first registered job (registration SHA-256 81398e6660c6538ebcf1566b3a2ebb6ecbaaefe29da074894848516b5749acda; a first registration was refused by its own budget guard after four burn jobs and is part of the deposit). Results, as they fell: of 13 field-on trials 11 resolved into one of the two images; the fraction resolved to the unicorn was 0.00, 0.00, 0.33, 0.50, 1.00, 1.00 for k = 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, a monotone curve with a single flip whose interpolated crossing lies at k* = 9.0; the censored decision time was 4.4 cycles at the two levels nearest the flip against 1.0 at the levels far from it; the two field-off controls, the same blend with the inter-domain coupling off, never resolved. The device's lean, read from the cycles in which the field was off, pointed to the heart and moved the fair point up by about one pixel, as the registered exploratory line asked. All five binding lines and the exploratory line held. The decision dynamics is the one a textbook predicts, a mean-field quench of 16 domains from the blend's magnetisation; the content of the experiment is that it runs, pre-registered to the pixel, on a quantum collective with the controller in the loop. Two chips were in the loop: the controller (ESP32-S3, with the field, the coupling matrix and the agents drawn on its display during the run) and a witness (ESP32-C3) running the byte-identical kernel source, compiled with the same arctangent and without fused multiply-add, so that the RISC-V chip in software arithmetic and the Xtensa chip with its floating-point unit produce the same bits: a seeded programme of 527 exchanges over every kernel path gave the same vector on both before the run, and on every one of the 148 ticks of the run the witness returned the same bytes as the controller. 148 jobs of 2048 shots, one device, one night. The deposit holds the registration (and the refused first registration with its burn log), the model and registration script, the runner, the verdict script, the kernel replica, the rehearsal on the noiseless simulator with both chips in the loop under the hashed registration, the run log with the measured populations of every qubit in every cycle and the witness flag of every tick, the job ids, the verdict (formed once), the bit-check vectors of the two chips, the write-up (buridan_paper_v1.pdf) and the scripts and figures that build it. The firmware sources and binaries are not deposited; their SHA-256 are in the registration.

title: Understanding and improving language models through interpretable decompositions
abstract: The interpretability of a machine learning model refers to the degree to which a human can understand the model's internal structures and reasoning processes. While the quality of natural language processing (NLP) models has traditionally been measured by predictive accuracy, this overlooks the demands of real-world deployment, where interpretability underpins trust and accountability in sensitive domains, supports systematic debugging, and enables the detection of undesirable biases. However, the scale of modern large language models (LLMs) and the distributed nature of their learned representations make it difficult to attribute any behavior to localized, human-understandable components. While local explanation methods can audit individual predictions, they neither reveal the global organization of a model's representations nor suggest what interventions might improve the model. This thesis investigates globally interpretable decompositions of language model representations, breaking opaque representations into human-interpretable components that can be understood and exploited for model improvement. We organize our investigation around three core constructs. Structures are the discrete computational patterns that organize how information is aggregated within a model's internals. Topics are the latent thematic variables that capture what a model or corpus is about. Features are the monosemantic directions in activation space that disentangle the concepts superimposed in model activations. Specifically, we propose a series of methods that discover and inject interpretable attention patterns as explicit priors, adaptively encode linguistic and dialogue structures through parameter-efficient adapters, align topic model training with the properties that make topics interpretable, recover the latent themes underlying LLM generation through explicit Bayesian inference, construct semantically grounded supervision from LLMs, and improve sparse dictionary learning through probabilistic feature selection and constrained optimization. A comprehensive set of experimental results demonstrates that our methods enhance not only the interpretability of language models, but also their performance, establishing interpretable decompositions as actionable foundations for both understanding and improving these models.

title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.

title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

evidence.title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
evidence.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. title: An Upper-Bound Inequality for the Calculation Time in Simulated Annealing: A Classical Analogue of the Adiabatic Theorem
abstract: It has recently been reported that classical systems have a speed limit for state evolution, although the concept of a speed limit had previously been considered to be unique to quantum systems. Owing to the speed limit for classical systems, a lower bound on the calculation time of simulated annealing for a desired calculation accuracy can be derived. However, such a lower bound does not provide a practical criterion for determining whether a calculation can be completed within a reasonable time. In this paper, we derive an inequality for classical systems analogous to the quantum adiabatic theorem, which provides a calculation time that guarantees a specified accuracy for fluctuation-exploiting computation. For a Fokker–Planck evolution with a spectral gap, the error is bounded by a relaxation term and, for a genuinely driven annealing protocol, by an additional driving term proportional to the speed of the instantaneous stationary distribution. The trade-off relation between calculation time and accuracy is given in a form that is tolerable for practical use. The result clarifies the roles of the relaxation gap and annealing speed, as well as the possible acceleration caused by detailed-balance-violating dynamics.

title: DHR-OD: Dynamic Heterogeneous Redundancy for Robust Object Detection
abstract: Object detection underpins safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving and intelligent surveillance, yet the inherent vulnerability of object detection models exposes them to the dual threat of adversarial and backdoor attacks. Existing defense methods are mostly passive, relying on prior knowledge of known attacks and thus failing to defend against unknown attacks. To address these problems, we introduce Dynamic Heterogeneous Redundancy (DHR) into object detection and build the Dynamic Heterogeneous Redundancy for robust Object Detection (DHR-OD) framework. DHR-OD defends against both threats through four modules, namely a heterogeneous executor pool, dynamic scheduling, multi-model arbitration, and closed-loop feedback, of which the multi-model arbitration module is the core. It fuses the box-level outputs of multiple heterogeneous detectors and identifies anomalies, turning the output differences among heterogeneous models into a defense. Experiments on COCO and PASCAL VOC show that DHR-OD retains 88.9% accuracy under PGD-20 attack and reduces the BadDet backdoor attack success rate from about 100% to about 35% without a dedicated detection module, making it a defense framework that covers both adversarial and backdoor threats while not relying on prior knowledge of specific attack forms.

title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.

title: Generated storm lifecycles fill the rare-event tail of short rainfall records
abstract: Historically rare ''one-in-a-generation'' storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, causing catastrophic damage and mounting casualties, and exposing the vulnerability of infrastructure designed around short observational records. To overcome the limitations of sparse data, we present StormGen, a generative machine-learning model that transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete, physically plausible hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes. Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, StormGen produced close counterparts for 4\5% of the most severe 2\% of storms--compared to just 3\% for stochastic storm transposition--and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. Crucially, from a single hour of initial rainfall, the model successfully reconstructed the specific lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey itself, despite the event being entirely absent in training. Because storm timing alone can more than double peak flows, these complete generated scenarios provide a vital mechanism to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes.

title: GNES: Neural-Guided Evolutionary Program Search for Interpretable UAV Swarm Control
abstract: Synthesizing interpretable velocity controllers for decentralized unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms requires optimizing discrete symbolic programs from sparse, expensive, long-horizon simulator feedback. Evolutionary program search preserves interpretability but often spends many evaluations on weak random variation, whereas deep multi-agent reinforcement learning can learn effective policies that are difficult to inspect. We propose GNES, a neural-guided evolutionary program search framework for symbolic UAV swarm controller synthesis. GNES casts controller design as a program-edit decision process: gene growth trees are program states, validity-preserving genetic operators are actions, simulator fitness provides the return, and policy–value graph neural networks learn edit signals over controller topology. Monte Carlo tree search performs look-ahead planning in controller-program space before simulator validation, closing the loop between evolution, learned guidance, and verified rollouts. Case studies on three simulated UAV swarm tasks produce compact, inspectable velocity controllers with non-obvious coordination motifs such as density-normalized radial gains and motion-compensating terms. In a six-method line-formation comparison over three seeds, every program-search variant exceeds the evolutionary and reinforcement-learning baselines on every seed with roughly one third of their evaluations, and ablations indicate that graph-structured policy–value learning and MCTS look-ahead each contribute, most visibly in search efficiency once final scores approach the task ceiling.

title: SPARK: Self-Correcting Embodied Memory via Physical Re-Observation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have seen growing adoption in embodied settings as language-queryable memories of the environment. However, existing approaches often assume a reliable single-episode knowledge base (KB) or accumulate observations across episodes without correcting prior errors. Such errors can persist through incorrect semantic labels, inaccurate object positions, and inconsistent spatial relationships. To address this, we present SPARK, a corrective multi-episode framework for embodied RAG. After the first episode, a semantic critic flags regions of the KB, a targeted planner generates revisits, and a selective merge adds, removes, or replaces KB information based on the new observations. We evaluate SPARK on four outdoor AirSim maps under two degraded viewpoint conditions, using perception-built KBs, a visibility-constrained oracle used only for evaluation, and a fixed set of 158 embodied question answering (EQA) questions scored before and after correction. A single corrective episode improves downstream EQA on every map under both conditions while storing 13-41% fewer objects than append-only updating, with gains up to 2.7x on one map-condition pair. Extending correction through Episode 4 brings every map above the EQA performance of its undegraded reference. Ablations show that the critic's three signals each contribute to performance, that targeted revisits achieve a larger mean gain than untargeted ones under the same budget, and that selective merging achieves gains comparable to append-only updating with a smaller KB. Overall, SPARK demonstrates the value of correcting embodied memory through targeted re-observation, particularly as embodied systems scale and the risk of accumulated errors increases.

title: CAPER: Circuit-Aware Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in LLMs for Analog Verification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate analog circuits, yet every netlist must also be verified. We propose LLMs as verification assistants for analog circuits that flag unmet specifications and reliability issues that appear under process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variation. These issues emerge from how circuit stages combine, a structure that generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA do not capture. To this end, we introduce CAPER, a circuit-aware PEFT method that adds a small branch alongside LoRA to read each stage's properties from the LLM and combine them from the relevant stages. In deciding whether a feedback loop is negative, LoRA and a high-rank adapter stay at chance, whereas CAPER answers every test case correctly. For comparator latches, where 11 of 90 LLM-written designs that work under nominal conditions fail under PVT variation, CAPER likewise learns to flag such latent failures, while generic adapters stay near chance. These results show that adding circuit knowledge to PEFT makes such analog verification checks learnable through fine-tuning.

title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory
abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.

title: Task-Performance Routing for Multi-Teacher Distillation in CT Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Pre-trained models offer complementary strengths in CT organ segmentation, but their relative accuracy varies across organs and spatial regions. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation can combine these strengths in a single student, yet global or instance-level teacher weights overlook variation within a 3D volume. We propose Task-Performance Routing (TPR), which uses region-wise segmentation errors to determine teacher weights during training without learned routing parameters. In hard regions, TPR favors teachers with lower prediction errors; in easy regions, it uses uniform weights to combine their knowledge. A hierarchical spatial partition provides fine-grained routing in shallow encoder stages and coarse-grained routing in deep stages. Experiments on BTCV, MSD-Liver, and MSD-Pancreas with two teacher pairs and two backbone architectures show higher Dice scores than the individual teachers, adaptive ensembles, and evaluated multi-teacher distillation baselines. On MSD-Pancreas, TPR achieves Dice scores of 65.40% with SwinUNETR and 68.25% with U-Net, compared with 64.38% and 67.45% for the corresponding adaptive ensembles. Inference uses the student alone, with no routing or teacher overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/EdvinCecilia/TPR_MultiTeacher.

title: Three instruments for evaluating AI audio tools: professional usefulness, creator-protection strength, and commercial disclosure
abstract: The three evaluation instruments used in the research report at 10.5281/zenodo.23476695, self-published and deposited in an open repository, with a DOI. They are a six-criterion Professional Usefulness scale with published anchors and a consent gate for voice technologies, a creator-protection evaluation with five columns and three 0-3 ratings, and a twenty-field commercial-disclosure checklist. They are published so that the report’s ratings can be checked, disputed or reproduced against the same anchors. The instruments have been applied by one analyst and have not been scored by a second rater. Section 7 gives the inter-rater protocol. Section 8 states the limitations, including that the band thresholds were reconstructed and may not reproduce every published rating, and that the creator-protection ratings are the author’s assessment, not legal advice.

title: PatchScout: Thematic Web Data Collection via Information Foraging
abstract: Researchers often need web corpora that are not answers to a single query, but reusable collections of documents spanning many decentralized sources. We refer to this problem as thematic web data collection: assembling semantically relevant documents that share a common theme but are scattered across heterogeneous and structurally disconnected regions of the web. Existing approaches, including traversal-based methods and LLM-driven web agents, are limited by local exploration or short-horizon stopping, preventing comprehensive collection. We formulate this task as a long-horizon information foraging problem over query-induced semantic patches, where the central challenge is deciding when to continue local exploitation and when to switch to new regions. We propose PatchScout, a multi-agent framework that instantiates a class of patch-switching policies to balance local exploitation and adaptive patch switching under a fixed budget. Experiments on four live-web topics show that PatchScout substantially improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented reasoning agent baselines. In an applied social science setting with an incomplete prior collection, PatchScout discovers 102 previously unidentified entities, illustrating its ability to expand existing thematic datasets.

title: On Statistical-Computational Gaps in Graph Combinatorial Testing Problems
abstract: We study high-dimensional graph combinatorial hypothesis testing problems in which a signal is supported on the edge set of an unknown subgraph drawn from a class invariant under vertex relabeling. For Gaussian observations, we characterize sharp statistical and computational thresholds (at polynomial order) for the signal magnitude required for strong detection across various combinatorial graph alternatives. Our analysis is based on bounding the second moments of the full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average, and coordinatewise maximum tests. Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture for computational hardness, we obtain planted-clique thresholds matching those known for Gaussian submatrix detection and identify new statistical-computational gaps for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. We also establish a novel transfer principle across natural exponential family observation models: matching the one-coordinate chi-square divergence preserves full likelihood-ratio second moments exactly and makes low-degree second moments equivalent up to constant factors under a degree condition. Under local regularity, we obtain corresponding testing upper bounds in terms of an effective signal strength. When these upper and lower bounds match, they yield universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime. As a consequence, statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdős--Rényi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.

Our analysis is based on bounding the second moments of the full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average, and coordinatewise maximum tests. Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture for computational hardness, we obtain planted-clique thresholds matching those known for Gaussian submatrix detection and identify new statistical-computational gaps for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. We also establish a novel transfer principle across natural exponential family observation models: matching the one-coordinate chi-square divergence preserves full likelihood-ratio second moments exactly and makes low-degree second moments equivalent up to constant factors under a degree condition. Under local regularity, we obtain corresponding testing upper bounds in terms of an effective signal strength. When these upper and lower bounds match, they yield universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime. As a consequence, statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdős--Rényi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.

title: Defining Page-Centric Visual Document Retrieval and Evaluating Existing Benchmarks
abstract: In modern information retrieval (IR), documents are increasingly encountered as structured sequences of visually rich, paginated units, rather than as flat text. Example documents encountered in our daily life include Word files, PDFs, and slide decks. Free text-centric retrieval systems either ignore this structure entirely or destroy it through arbitrary passage chunking. In this paper, we formulate page-centric Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) with pages as the fundamental indexing units and document context available for assessing page relevance. The formulation distinguishes two retrieval granularities, page and document, and three retrieval paradigms: independent-item, evidence-set, and iterative retrieval. We then assess 42 benchmarks using eight criteria covering corpus characteristics, query construction, relevance annotation, and ranking support. Our analysis shows two main findings on current VDR research. First, evaluation remains concentrated on page-level independent-item retrieval, with fewer resources supporting document-level, evidence-set, and iterative settings. Second, queries originating from real user information needs independently of target corpus content and graded relevance judgments are uncommon, while the coverage and verification of relevance judgments vary substantially. Both findings reveal gaps between the capabilities applications require and those existing evaluation protocols can establish. We provide benchmark selection guidance and identify priorities for future benchmark design, emphasizing alignment between task requirements, relevance semantics, and evaluation protocols.

title: A Domain Label Is Not a Treatment: Why Specialist and General-Purpose Language Models Trade Places Across Studies, What a 'Medical' Checkpoint Leaves Unspecified, and the Matched Contrasts That Would Assign the Gain
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A September 2026 study compares an 8B general-purpose instruction-tuned model with a medically fine-tuned checkpoint built on the same base and finds that the general model scores higher both at selecting the meaning of medical jargon and at recognising when a word is being used as jargon, significantly so on the second, and that the medical checkpoint's deficit on the second task sits in a few pre-existing components it over-weights. The finding joins a run of 2024-2026 results in which medical models fail to beat their bases, set against an older and still-growing record in which domain-adapted models in code, mathematics, chip design, law and clinical text beat general ones by wide margins. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these verdicts are not answers to one question, because a specialist-versus-generalist comparison is indexed by five things that the studies set differently: the treatment (what was trained, on how much text the base had not already seen), the comparator (the starting checkpoint, a post-trained sibling, or a model of another lineage), the elicitation (whose prompt format and whose decision threshold), the target skill (recall, terminology, extraction against labels, or multi-step computation), and the statistic (paired tests, intervals, calibration). Read through those indices, the negative medical results hold in one well-populated cell - a modest post-training or continued-pretraining treatment on a web-trained base, compared with a strong sibling under independent prompting on recall or terminology - and the large positive results hold in cells where the domain data are large relative to the base's exposure, absent from the public web, or labelled for the exact task. The paper argues that the anchor's mechanistic result is better read as a shifted decision prior than as lost knowledge, consolidates 27 published results in a table, maps fourteen studies onto four of the five indices, states a classification procedure, and specifies five matched contrasts that would decide what a domain label buys.

title: FeDLRT: Federated Dynamical Low-Rank Training
abstract: Abstract. We propose a federated dynamical low-rank training (FeDLRT) scheme to reduce client compute and communication costs—two significant performance bottlenecks in horizontal federated learning. Our method builds upon dynamical low-rank time integration schemes for manifold-constrained optimization to create a global low-rank basis of network weights, which enables client training on a small coefficient matrix. This global low-rank basis allows us to incorporate a variance correction scheme and prove global loss descent and convergence to a stationary point on a low-rank manifold. FeDLRT features dynamic augmentation and truncation of the low-rank bases to optimize computing and communication resource utilization. Notably FeDLRT only trains a small coefficient matrix per client. We demonstrate the efficiency of FeDLRT in an array of computer vision benchmarks with both independent and identically distributed (IID) and non-IID data and show a reduction of client compute and communication costs by up to an order of magnitude with minimal impacts on global accuracy. FeDLRT performs as well as classical methods such as FedAvg and FedLin, with a fraction of the memory and compute requirements.

title: Efficient NPN Classification for Large Functions using Graph Neural Network
abstract: Two Boolean functions are considered NPN equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs, or negating the output. Efficient NPN classification is valuable in fields such as logic synthesis, quantum computing, and information theory. However, exact NPN classification demands exhaustive enumeration of all possible input permutations and negations. Its complexity grows exponentially, making it impractical for larger functions with more inputs. In this paper, we introduce the first learning-based formulation for NPN classification by recasting it as NPN action prediction. Our method represents Boolean functions as AND-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and applies a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network to predict input negations, output negation, and input permutations. To mitigate the non-canonicity of logic networks, we further introduce graph rewriting techniques that reduce structural ambiguity and recover useful symmetries before prediction. Experimental results show that NPN action prediction is learnable, that the resulting canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines, and that on practical benchmarks our method approaches exact methods on tractable cases while scaling to functions with up to 16 inputs.

title: OT-CAL: Optimal-Transport-Guided Adaptive Sample Selection for Efficient Visual Learning
abstract: Deep neural networks for image recognition are typically trained using mini-batches, with a forward pass to compute predictions and losses followed by a more computationally expensive backward pass to update model parameters. However, not all training samples contribute equally to learning, suggesting that computation can be reduced by performing backward passes only on informative samples. The challenge is that sample informativeness changes throughout training: difficult samples may be valuable early on, improving samples become important later, and class diversity becomes increasingly relevant toward the end. Existing methods often rely on fixed selection rules or computationally expensive per-sample gradient calculations. We propose OT-CAL, an adaptive data selection method that automatically adjusts its sampling preferences during training. OT-CAL represents each sample using five informativeness features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty. A curriculum vector describes the currently preferred sample characteristics, and optimal-transport-based matching assigns selection weights according to how closely samples match this target. The curriculum vector is then updated using the selected samples, forming a feedback loop that adapts without a manually defined schedule. Experiments on three standard visual learning benchmarks show that, when selecting 50% of each mini-batch, OT-CAL improves performance by 1.3--2.1 points over AdaSelection while achieving 1.18--1.24 times faster training than full-data training.

title: LEAP: Efficient LLM Inference Scheduling with Generalizable Length Prediction
abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.

title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents
abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.

title: Grounding Multimodal Reasoning with Evidence-Ablated Negatives
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/DawnLIU35/EVAN.git.

title: AgentHeal: Evaluating Goal-Preserving Resource Recovery of Web Agents under Access Barriers
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating complex information-seeking and transactional tasks across the open web. However, their real-world reliability remains limited by access barriers, such as dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses. These barriers block the primary execution path, causing agents to abort prematurely, loop indefinitely, or quietly compromise the user's original constraints. Existing evaluations either implicitly assume that target resources are freely accessible or focus on transient perturbations that simple retries can resolve, failing to capture scenarios where agents must actively reroute around impassable bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces AgentHeal, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating goal-preserving resource recovery, defined as the ability of web agents to detect non-transient access barriers, pivot to legitimate alternative sources, and fulfill the user's exact original objective. Spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay, our experiments on leading LLM backbones show that average task success drops sharply from 89.4% to 43.7% under access barriers. Further analysis reveals that agents frequently fall for deceptive look-alikes, fail to escalate to users when necessary, violate access policies, or waste computation on futile retries, providing actionable diagnostics for developing resilient web agents.

title: XLaw-JP-27B: A Lightweight Open Model Specialized for Japanese Law
abstract: We present XLaw-JP-27B, an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law that runs on a single 48\,GB GPU under the Apache~2.0 licence. It adapts Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. We evaluate it on eight Japanese legal tasks---the multiple-choice section of the bar examination in 2024, 2025 and 2026, statement-level bar questions (JBE-QA), statute questions (LawQA-JP), the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting built from government model contracts---against open models of 12--33B under identical prompts and retrieval. XLaw-JP-27B ranks first on six tasks, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 against 2.8--3.1 for the baselines). It is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175, meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used in training), while open Japanese 32--33B models fail at least one year. A controlled study of each component shows that retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, and that thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition and more self-distillation do not. The largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law. The model is available as a free web service at https://x-law.jp/ with the weights available at https://huggingface.co/X-LawJapan/xlaw-jp-27b under Apache~2.0.
